e.t: This word means “good,” describing something beneficial, right, or worthy of approval. It can refer to what is good itself, to a good person or doer, or to the practice of doing good. In the Greek New Testament, it is used broadly across 102 occurrences, including statements about good actions, good character, and what people recognize as good. Its exact force—whether describing a person, action, or thing—comes from the sentence where it appears, but its central sense remains goodness rather than harm or evil.

This word describes something unswerving or unwavering—steady rather than turning aside or changing direction. It expresses firmness and constancy, especially when a person or commitment must remain settled. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 10:23. The word itself gives the sense of holding firmly and consistently, while the surrounding verse determines exactly how that steadfastness is applied there.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to appoint,” “to appoint” someone or something, or “to show.” It describes an action of assigning or making something known, depending on how it functions in a sentence. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 10:1 and Acts 1:24. Its approved meanings include both appointment and showing, so the surrounding sentence determines which aspect is most prominent. These uses present it as an active verb expressing what someone does rather than naming a person, object, or quality.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to arise,” “to get up,” or to be raised. It describes someone moving from a seated, lying, or lowered position to an upright one, and it can also describe rising in response to a direction or situation. The word appears 108 times in the Greek New Testament, so its exact force depends on the surrounding sentence. It is used throughout the New Testament, especially in Acts and Luke, for ordinary movement as well as significant acts of rising.

e.t: This word means “to become callous” or “to lose all sensitivity,” describing a person who has become emotionally and morally unresponsive. It points to a deep hardening in which a person no longer reacts with proper feeling or concern. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Ephesians 4:19, so its broader use cannot be traced through multiple passages. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea is the loss of inward sensitivity.

e.t: This word means “give” or “pay”: it describes handing something over or providing what is owed. Its sense is practical and transactional, but the same action word can also describe giving in a broader sense, depending on the sentence. It occurs 48 times in the Greek New Testament, across 46 verses, so readers will meet it in varied settings rather than in only one repeated expression. The central idea remains the act of giving or paying something to someone.

Armageddon is a proper name, preserved in English as “Armageddon,” rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named subject in the Greek New Testament. This word occurs once in that corpus, in Revelation 16:16. The name itself gives the basic lexical meaning; its precise significance and role depend on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This Greek New Testament word means “flute,” referring to a musical wind instrument. It identifies the instrument itself rather than an action or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at 1 Corinthians 14:7. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a flute or similar instrument used to produce music. This word describes someone who has condemned himself or herself, rather than merely receiving a judgment from another person. It expresses personal responsibility for standing under condemnation. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Titus 3:11, and its precise force there is understood from the surrounding passage. Its central idea remains clear: a self-condemned person has brought condemnation upon himself through his own settled course or conduct.

Bernice is a personal name, referring to a specific individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears three times, and each occurrence is rendered “Bernice.” All three occurrences are in Acts: Acts 25:13, Acts 25:23, and Acts 26:30. The name itself identifies the person; the surrounding passage supplies the details of her role in each scene.

This word means “an old man” or “old person.” It is a noun used to identify a male person by advanced age, rather than to name a separate office, title, or spiritual role. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at John 3:4. Its basic lexical force is simply a reference to an older man or person; the surrounding sentence determines how that reference functions in context.

This word refers to “leather” or “skin,” describing the material itself rather than a person or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 11:37. Its basic meaning identifies animal skin or leather as a physical material. The word alone does not specify how that material is being used; the surrounding verse and passage provide that particular detail.

Justification means being declared right or accepted as righteous. In the New Testament, this word names the resulting standing of those whom God counts as right, rather than describing a human achievement or personal claim. It is a noun expressing the status or act of being justified. This word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, both times in Romans, where its precise force is understood from the surrounding discussion. Its direct English rendering is “justification.”

This word describes someone or something that is a hundred years old. It expresses an age of one hundred years rather than a general idea of being old. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Romans 4:19. Because the word occurs only there and the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise role in that sentence must be understood from the passage itself; its basic meaning remains a specific age: “a hundred years old.”

This Greek New Testament word means “before.” It indicates that something comes earlier than another thing or is positioned in front of someone or something, depending on the sentence. It appears two times in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 1:8 and Acts 8:21. Its basic idea is relational: it places a person, action, or circumstance ahead of another in time or position. The surrounding verse determines which sense is intended in a particular occurrence.

This word means “a promise”: a declared assurance about something that will be given or accomplished. It is a noun, so it names the promise itself rather than the act of promising. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Peter—once in the plural and once in the singular. Its basic meaning remains the same whether referring to several promises or one particular promise. The surrounding passage determines what promised matter is in view in each verse.

This word is the personal name “Eve.” It functions as a proper name, identifying Eve when she is mentioned in the Greek New Testament. The word occurs twice in this corpus, once in 2 Corinthians and once in 1 Timothy, and both occurrences are rendered “Eve.” Because it is a name rather than a general description, its meaning is primarily identification: it points to the individual called Eve. The surrounding verse supplies the specific purpose of mentioning her in each passage.

This word describes something “easily entangling” or “thwarting”—something that readily ensnares a person or gets in the way. It points to an obstacle that can hinder movement or progress, rather than simply describing ordinary difficulty. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 12:1. The precise force of the word in that verse is understood through its surrounding sentence and passage, but its basic sense is something that entangles or obstructs.

e.t: This word means “to forfeit” or “to lose”—to suffer the loss of something valuable or fail to retain it. It can describe losing a benefit, possession, or desired outcome. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, including passages about gaining the world while losing one’s true good, suffering loss, and counting former advantages as loss. The word therefore carries the straightforward idea of something being lost or forfeited, while the surrounding sentence identifies what is at stake.

This word means “daughter” or “daughters,” referring to a female child in relation to her parent or family. It is a noun used for one daughter or for more than one daughter, depending on the sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 28 times, showing that it is a normal family term used across several books. Its meaning remains centered on a daughter as a female descendant or family member; the surrounding passage determines the specific relationship being described.

This word means “atoning sacrifice” or “propitiation.” It is a noun that names the sacrifice connected with making atonement. In its two occurrences in the Greek New Testament, it appears in 1 John, where the word identifies what Christ is in relation to sin and reconciliation. The central idea is not merely an offering, but an offering understood as dealing with the need for atonement. Its precise force in either verse is clarified by the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains an atoning sacrifice.

e.t: “Perhaps” expresses possibility rather than certainty. It presents something as a consideration that may or may not happen, without declaring it definite. This Greek New Testament word occurs once, in Luke 20:13, so its normal meaning is established from that single occurrence and the gloss “perhaps,” while the surrounding verse supplies its particular force there. It functions as a concise word of uncertainty, leaving room for an outcome or possibility without treating it as assured.

e.t: To condemn means to declare someone guilty or deserving judgment. It can describe an act of judging another person, announcing a sentence, or stating the outcome that follows guilt. In the Greek New Testament, this word appears 18 times, including uses rendered “condemn” and “condemned.” Its exact force—whether referring to a person’s judgment, a legal sentence, or final accountability—depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This word means “horn” or “horns,” referring to the pointed projection of an animal. In the New Testament, it can describe one horn or several horns, depending on the passage. The word occurs 11 times in the Greek New Testament, with 10 occurrences in Revelation and one in Luke. Because horns appear in visions and prophetic scenes, the surrounding verse and passage are needed to determine whether the word is being used literally or as part of an image.

This word means “Laodicea,” the proper name of a place named in the Greek New Testament. It is not a description or action word, but a name used to identify Laodicea in several passages. The word occurs six times, all in the New Testament corpus: four times in Colossians and twice in Revelation. Its first recorded occurrence is in Colossians 2:1 and its last is in Revelation 3:14.

This word means “smooth,” describing something that is even rather than rough or uneven. It functions as a descriptive word, identifying the surface or condition of something. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, in Luke 3:5. Its basic sense is therefore focused and specific: it portrays smoothness, with the surrounding verse needed to show exactly what is being described there.

e.h: Lycia, a Region of Asia Minor
e.t: Lycia is the name of a region on the southwestern coast of Asia Minor. It functions as a place-name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 27:5. The name identifies a location within the travel account, while the surrounding passage supplies the details of the journey. Thus, its basic meaning is simply “Lycia,” the geographic region named in that verse.

Melchizedek is a personal name, referring to the person called Melchizedek in the Greek New Testament. The word is not presented as a general quality, action, or object; it identifies one particular biblical figure. It occurs eight times in the Greek New Testament, all within Hebrews, where the name is repeated in passages discussing priesthood. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the name itself remains a personal designation.

This Greek New Testament word marks a question, often expecting the answer “no?” or expressing the comparison “how much more.” It helps frame a question rather than naming a person, thing, action, or quality. In some sentences it is not translated into English because its force is carried by the question itself. It occurs 18 times in the Greek New Testament, from Matthew through James. Its precise force depends on the surrounding question.

“Nazarene” means a person from Nazareth, or someone identified with that place. It functions as a name or description connected with Nazareth rather than expressing an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs six times, all in Mark and Luke. Its use identifies Jesus by his association with Nazareth, while the surrounding verse supplies the particular sense in each passage.

This word means “fasting”. It names the practice of going without food for a period of time. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, referring to fasting as a recognized religious practice or as a hardship endured. Its meaning remains focused on abstaining from food, while the surrounding passage determines the purpose or circumstances. The word appears in Luke, Acts, and 2 Corinthians, showing its use across different New Testament settings.

e.t: This word means “to guide,” “to lead,” or “guides”—to direct someone along a path or toward a destination. It describes active direction, whether a person is being led by another or being brought forward under guidance. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, with this guiding sense appearing across Matthew, Luke, John, Acts, and Revelation. Its precise force in a particular sentence depends on who is guiding and whom or what is being led.

e.t: This word means to heap insults on someone or to revile them. It describes openly abusive speech that attacks a person’s honor rather than offering a fair correction. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs nine times, including descriptions of people being reviled or insulted. The sense can include harsh, contemptuous words spoken against someone because of their connection to Jesus or because of their actions. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

e.h: What Kind Of or What Sort
e.t: This word means “what kind of” or “what sort”. It asks about the nature, character, or quality of a person, thing, or matter. Rather than merely asking what something is, it asks what it is like or what category it belongs to. In the Greek New Testament, it appears five times, showing a focused use as a question or description of character and kind. Its meaning remains dependent on the noun or subject being considered in each sentence. The word appears in Acts, 1 Corinthians, Galatians, 1 Thessalonians, and James.

me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: It means “correctly,” describing an action, statement, or judgment done in the right way. As an adverb, it tells how something is done rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, each occurrence appearing in a different verse. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on what action or words it modifies, but its central sense remains straightforward: something is done accurately, properly, or in agreement with what is right.

This word expresses negation: “no” or “not.” It is used to deny, reject, or indicate that something does not happen, exist, or apply. In some sentences, its meaning extends to “no one,” when it denies a person or group. As a very common Greek New Testament word, it appears 1,610 times, so its precise force depends on the word or statement it negates. It occurs throughout the New Testament, from Matthew through Revelation, and normally serves as a concise negative particle rather than naming an object or action.

Pamphylia is the name of a region mentioned in the New Testament. It identifies a geographic place rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual condition. The word appears five times in the Greek New Testament, all in Acts, and each occurrence refers to Pamphylia. Acts mentions it alongside other locations connected with travel, preaching, or the movement of people. Since it is a proper place name, its meaning is simply the region it designates; the surrounding verse explains what happened there or why it is mentioned.

“Paul” is a personal name identifying a man in the New Testament. It functions as a proper name rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. The name appears 158 times in the Greek New Testament, in 154 verses, with most occurrences in Acts. It continues to identify the same named person in several New Testament letters, including 2 Peter, where its final occurrence appears.

This word describes involvement in magic or meddlesome interference in matters that do not properly belong to a person. Its two occurrences in the Greek New Testament use the related ideas of magical practice and intrusive busyness, showing a range from occult activity to improper interference. It appears in Acts 19:19 and 1 Timothy 5:13; the surrounding verse context determines which aspect is emphasized in each passage.

“Platter” means a broad, usually shallow dish used to hold or serve food. In the Greek New Testament, this word refers to that kind of serving dish rather than to the food itself. It occurs five times in five verses, and each occurrence is rendered “platter.” Its ordinary meaning is concrete and household-related: a vessel on which food can be placed and presented.

Puteoli is the name of a place. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Acts 28:13, and English Bible translations preserve it as “Puteoli” rather than translating it as a descriptive word. As a proper name, it identifies a specific location mentioned in the account. The word itself does not describe an action, quality, or spiritual principle; its function is to name the place. The surrounding verse and passage provide the details about what happened there.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means to accuse someone, make a charge beforehand, or say that a charge has already been made. It describes the act of bringing an accusation against a person rather than merely noticing a fault. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Romans 3:9. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is the formal or deliberate raising of an accusation.

me: Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, second, Plural

e.t: This word means “to touch,” describing physical contact with someone or something. It is a verb that expresses the act of making contact rather than merely seeing, approaching, or speaking. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 11:46. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is the straightforward action of touching. This word should therefore be understood as an expression of contact.

This word means “prophetic,” describing something connected with prophecy or carrying the character of prophecy. It functions as a describing word rather than naming a person or object by itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice: once in Romans and once in 2 Peter. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central meaning remains a connection with prophecy.

Rhoda is a personal name used to identify an individual, rather than a word expressing an action, quality, or object. It is rendered “Rhoda” and appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 12:13. Because it is a name, its meaning here is primarily identification: it tells the reader who a person is, while the surrounding passage supplies the person’s role and actions. The name itself does not describe a general spiritual principle or idea.

e.t: This word means “to deliver” or “to rescue”—to bring someone out of danger, trouble, or an oppressive situation. It can describe deliverance already given, a request for rescue, or a future act of saving. The central idea is removal from a threatening condition into safety or freedom. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 17 times, showing repeated use for people being delivered from danger, distress, or hostile powers. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to worship” and can describe someone who “worshiped.” It refers to the act of giving worship within a sentence. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Romans 1:25. Its basic meaning remains the act of worship; the precise force of the word in that sentence depends on the surrounding verse and passage. This is a past-tense rendering in that occurrence, describing an act that was performed.

e.t: This word means “to draw.” It is a verb describing the act of pulling or drawing something from one place or position. Its basic meaning remains simple and action-focused, without requiring a particular object or direction apart from the surrounding sentence. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, once in Mark 14:47 and once in Acts 16:27. The immediate sense in either passage depends on what is being drawn and the surrounding context.

e.t: This word means “to share” or “to share with,” expressing the act of participating in or receiving something together with others. It describes sharing rather than keeping something solely for oneself, and its wording can point to a shared portion or participation. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 9:13. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is sharing in something with others.

me: Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to correspond” or “to correspond to,” expressing a relationship in which something matches, aligns with, or stands alongside something else. It is a verb describing correspondence rather than naming an object or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Galatians 4:25. The surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain precisely what is being compared there, but the word itself centers on agreement or matching between related things.

Misery refers to a condition of distress, suffering, or wretchedness. It describes the painful state a person experiences rather than an action they perform. In the Greek New Testament, this word appears twice, rendered “misery” in both occurrences, including Romans 3:16 and James 5:1. Its exact force in either verse is determined by the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the experience of severe hardship or sorrow.

The word means “hymn,” referring to a song intended to be sung. It functions as a noun, naming a kind of song rather than an action or a person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Ephesians 5:19 and Colossians 3:16. Its basic meaning is therefore a hymn or sung composition, while the precise role it plays in either verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage.

This word means “anointing,” referring to the act or result of applying oil or another substance in an anointing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in two verses of 1 John 2. Its basic meaning remains focused on anointing itself rather than on a broader idea supplied by the word alone. The surrounding sentence and passage determine the specific force of the reference, but the word’s central sense is clear and consistent.
